context: fast-track finishing & MEP-led · shell-and-core interface · snagging-heavy

brief.intro: An office or commercial interior fit-out builds inside a shell your client doesn't own the structure of — the landlord has already delivered the base building (structure, façade, core, lifts and risers), and your scope is everything inside it: partitions, ceilings, raised floor, finishes, MEP terminal units and furniture. New to this type? The programme is not driven by construction difficulty but by two things — how fast a frozen interior design turns into ordered long-lead furniture and joinery, and how much the landlord's approval process (technical review, permits, work-hour restrictions in an occupied building) adds to the front end. Fit-outs are almost always fast-track and compressed against a lease or move-in date, so the finishing-to-MEP interface must be resolved early rather than discovered as clashes later. Because the space is fully visible and often sits beside occupied neighbours, quality control and snagging carry more weight per square metre than on a new building shell.

scope.desc: De-snag and practical completion / handover to the tenant.

glossary.plain: the base building the landlord hands over — structure, façade, lifts and riser capacity, but no interior fit-out.
CAT A is the landlord's baseline fit-out (ceiling grid, raised floor, basic MEP); CAT B is the tenant's full fit-out — partitions, finishes, furniture — which is this project.
"No Objection Certificate" — the landlord's written approval needed before certain works, especially MEP tie-ins, can proceed.
variable-air-volume box / fan-coil unit — the terminal unit in the ceiling that delivers conditioned air to a zone.
a floor built on pedestals above the structural slab, so power and data cabling run underneath it.
the landlord's building-wide system (fire alarm, BMS, risers) that the fit-out taps into rather than replaces.
recording, then closing out, defects before handover.
the point the space is handed over fit for occupation, snag list notwithstanding.

must_get_right: Confirm the shell & core handover condition and the landlord's approval (NOC) process before design freeze — waiting on landlord sign-off, not construction, is the classic early delay.
Size the MEP fit-out against base-building capacity (chilled water, power, floor loading, riser space) before ordering — exceeding it forces a redesign mid-programme.
Order long-lead furniture, joinery and specialist finishes against a frozen design, not the move-in date — late design changes are the single biggest schedule risk on a fit-out.
Protect real time for MEP testing/balancing and snagging at the end — fast-track programmes compress this first, and it shows at handover.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Because the programme is short and fast-track, activities are often modelled in days rather than weeks, and the network is calculated (F9) with total float kept ≥ 0 against the lease/move-in date.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Works typically run within the landlord's permitted hours for an occupied building — often extended evening or weekend shifts for noisy trades (demolition, drilling) — with a separate after-hours calendar for base-building tie-ins and lift/riser access.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs design freeze & landlord NOC → strip-out → partitions/ceilings → MEP first fix → floor & wall finishes → MEP second fix & devices → joinery/FF&E → testing & balancing → snagging → landlord sign-off. Structure is absent from this type; the true drivers are design-freeze timing, landlord approvals and long-lead furniture/joinery.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Interior design and finishes are frozen before ordering long-lead furniture and joinery; the base-building shell, risers and plant capacity are as surveyed at handover; landlord technical approvals are granted within a stated review period; a single tenant decision-maker handles variations.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: Long-lead furniture, joinery and specialist fixtures are tracked as milestones and typically set the true critical path on a fit-out:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Work in an occupied or multi-tenant building constrains hours, lift use, material deliveries and noisy trades; loading-dock and freight-lift bookings are shared with other tenants and must be programmed early. Landlord technical review adds a fixed lead time ahead of MEP tie-ins.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: late design freeze delaying long-lead orders, a landlord approval or tie-in permit slipping the start of MEP works, and clashes discovered late between ceiling services and the finishing design. Contingency is held before furniture/joinery delivery and before snagging.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1–2 to the tenant/landlord; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4 for daily trade sequencing on a compressed, fast-track programme — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
